title: Event Triggered Execution: Udev Rules
summary: Udev is the Linux kernel device manager, and its user-space helper, systemd-udevd, creates and removes device nodes, controls access to the pseudo-device files under the dev directory and reacts to hardware events such as a disk or a keyboard being attached. Rules are read from several directories, including the etc, run, usr lib and lib locations, and each rule combines match keys, which describe the event, with action keys, which describe the response. Root permission is required to write those files, and priority is decided by the directory and by the numeric prefix in the file name. An adversary adds or edits a rule so that a chosen device event, or even access to a pseudo-device, runs their binary. Because the daemon gives each job a short lifetime inside a sandbox without network or filesystem access, a common pattern is to detach the payload in the background from the run action. The artefacts are new or modified rule files, worker processes under the device daemon that spawn shells or binaries, and payloads that escape the sandbox. Production hosts normally have a small, static rule set, so a recent addition is the key discriminator.

beginner.definition: This technique uses Linux device rules to start an attacker's program. On Linux a service called udev notices when hardware is added or removed. It reads rule files that say what to do when a device event happens. An attacker with root access adds a rule that starts their own program. The program then runs when the chosen event occurs. This sub-technique differs from its parent because a hardware or device event, and not a sign in, sets off the code.
beginner.whyItMatters: Rule files live in protected folders, so writing one shows that the attacker already has root. The rule then keeps the code alive in a place most administrators do not check. Device events happen often, so the attacker's program can start many times a day. If you never compare rule files with a known good set, a quiet rule can keep an intruder on the server for a long time.
howItWorks: On Linux the kernel device manager, called udev, notices when hardware is added or removed.
It reads rule files from several folders, and each rule has a match part and an action part.
The match part describes a condition, such as a device name or a device event.
The action part says what to do, and one common action is to run a command.
An attacker with root writes a rule that runs their program on a chosen device event.
The device manager allows only short tasks, so the attacker starts their program in the background.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel where every door sensor reports to a small control room. The control room follows a printed list that says if the store room door opens, switch on the light. If someone adds a line to that list, the control room will open a side gate whenever any door moves. Udev rules are that printed list, and only staff with root access can edit it.
takeaways: Udev rules connect a hardware event to a command on Linux.
Only root can write rule files, so a new rule means high access was already held.
Watch for device manager workers that start shells or detached background programs.

objectives: Explain what udev does and how rule files are organised.
Describe the difference between match keys and action keys.
Name the directories that hold rule files and explain how priority is decided.
Identify telemetry for rule changes and device manager child processes.
Explain how the sandbox around device manager jobs is avoided by detaching a process.
Compare a normal rule set with an attacker's addition.
